# AI Services - LangChain4J - Ollama

[`AiServices`](https://github.com/langchain4j/langchain4j/blob/main/langchain4j/src/main/java/dev/langchain4j/service/AiServices.java)
in LangChain4J is a powerful abstraction layer that enables you to define a Java
interface, annotate its methods with prompts, and have LangChain4J automatically
generate an implementation to handle communication with LLMs (e.g., OpenAI,
Ollama). It manages prompt templating, model invocation, chat memory, structured
inputs and outputs, streaming, tool calling, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation
(RAG). It serves as a declarative, more flexible replacement for Chains, with
reduced boilerplate.

This example demonstrates how to use `AiServices` to perform several simple
tasks. Both user messages (`@UserMessage`) and system messages
(`@SystemMessage`) are supported. These annotations use templates and therefore
allow variable substitution.

Please note that the `AiService` feature is not currently supported by Spring AI.

Below is an example of a date service that provides the necessary implementation
to perform the task.

```java
package demo.services;

import dev.langchain4j.service.SystemMessage;
import dev.langchain4j.service.UserMessage;
import dev.langchain4j.service.V;

import java.time.LocalDateTime;

public interface DateTimeService {
    @SystemMessage("Extract and only return the date and time from the given text in the format: ISO 8601 Format")
    @UserMessage("{{text}}.")
    LocalDateTime extractDateTimeFrom(@V("text") String text);
}
```

**How does this work?**

Consider the following example:

```java
final ChatModel chatModel = OllamaChatModel.builder()
        .modelName("llama3")
        .baseUrl("http://localhost:11434/")
        .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(60))
        .build();

final DateTimeService service = AiServices.builder(DateTimeService.class)
                .chatModel(chatModel)
                .build();

final String text = "Apollo 11 landed on the Moon on July 20, 1969 at 20:17:40 UTC";
final LocalDateTime dateTime = service.extractDateTimeFrom(text);
```

LangChain4J provides an implementation of `DateTimeService` that embeds the
method parameters into the user message.

The method call:

```java
extractDateTimeFrom("Apollo 11 landed on the Moon on July 20, 1969 at 20:17:40 UTC");
```

is converted into a **single prompt** sent to the model, following the
`@UserMessage` template.

Substituting `{{text}}` with the argument:

```
Extract and only return the date and time from: Apollo 11 landed on the Moon on July 20, 1969 at 20:17:40 UTC.
```

This **exact string** is sent as the **user message** to the model. No
additional hidden messages are sent unless system messages have been explicitly
configured.

**How many requests are made to the model?**

Only **one request** (one API call) is made per method invocation.

The process is as follows:

1. LangChain4J constructs the user prompt from the template.
2. It sends a **single request** to the model with that prompt.
3. The model returns a **text response** (ideally just the date-time string).
4. LangChain4J attempts to parse the returned string into a `LocalDateTime`.

If the model responds with `"1969-07-20T20:17:40"`, LangChain4J converts it into
a `LocalDateTime`.

**Does LangChain4J perform multiple validation calls?**

No. By default, `AiServices` makes **only one call**. If parsing fails (for
example, if the model returns `"July 20, 1969 20:17:40 UTC"` instead of ISO
format), you may configure **output parsers** or add custom logic to clean the
response. This processing still occurs after the single API call.

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 25](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)

- [Ollama](https://ollama.com/download)

## Run the example

1. Download and setup Ollama

   If you haven’t already, please download and install Ollama from the
   [official download page](https://ollama.com/download), following the
   instructions provided. Ollama includes a command-line tool for managing and
   interacting with it.

   Models must be downloaded from a repository, such as the
   [Ollama Library](https://ollama.com/library) or
   [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/models). Ensure the model is saved in
   a supported format, such as
   [GPT-Generated Unified Format (GGUF)](https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/gguf).

   To list models installed locally, run:

   ```shell
   ollama list
   ```

   After a fresh installation, no models will be listed.

   ```
   NAME    ID    SIZE    MODIFIED
   ```

   To get started, download [LLaMA 3.1](https://ollama.com/library/llama3.1)
   with:

   ```shell
   ollama pull llama3.1
   ```

   This process may take a few seconds to several minutes, depending on your
   internet connection.

   Once the model is downloaded, you can begin using it.

   (*Optional*) To confirm the model has been installed, list the models again:

   ```shell
   ollama list
   ```

   You should now see `llama3.1` in the list.

   ```
   NAME               ID              SIZE      MODIFIED
   llama3.1:latest    46e0c10c039e    4.9 GB    Less than a second ago
   ```

   To interact with the model using the command-line interface, run:

   ```
   ollama run llama3.1
   ```

   This opens a prompt where you can engage with the model. If the model has not
   yet been downloaded, Ollama will download it automatically. You can interact
   with the model via the CLI

   ```
   >>> When did humans first land on the Moon?

   Humans first landed on the Moon on July 20, 1969, during the Apollo 11 mission. The spacecraft carrying the astronauts, Neil Armstrong and Edwin "Buzz" Aldrin, landed on the lunar surface in the Sea of Tranquility at 20:17 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time). Armstrong became the first person to set foot on the Moon, famously declaring "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind" as he stepped out of the lunar module Eagle.

   >>> /bye
   ```

   Alternatively, you can interact with the model through a graphical interface,
   such as [Open WebUI](https://github.com/open-webui/open-webui), which offers
   a web-based experience similar to cloud-hosted models.

   To verify that Ollama is running and accessible on the default port `11434`,
   use:

   ```shell
   curl --silent --show-error 'http://localhost:11434/api/tags' | jq
   ```

   This will return a list of available models.

   ```
   {
     "models": [
       {
         "name": "llama3.1:latest",
         "model": "llama3.1:latest",
         "modified_at": "2077-04-27T11:34:56.789000000Z",
         "size": 4920753328,
         "digest": "46e0c10c039e019119339687c3c1757cc81b9da49709a3b3924863ba87ca666e",
         "details": {
           "parent_model": "",
           "format": "gguf",
           "family": "llama",
           "families": [
             "llama"
           ],
           "parameter_size": "8.0B",
           "quantization_level": "Q4_K_M"
         }
       }
     ]
   }
   ```

   When using Ollama via the REST API, as in the following steps, the required
   model must be downloaded in advance. Ollama does not automatically download
   missing models when accessed through the REST API; this functionality is only
   available via the CLI, for example with `ollama run llama3.1`. Please ensure
   the `llama3.1` model is available before proceeding.

   ```shell
   curl 'http://localhost:11434/api/chat' \
     --silent \
     --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
     --data '{
     "model": "llama3.1",
     "messages": [
       {
         "role": "user",
         "content": "When did humans first land on the Moon?"
       }
     ],
     "stream": false,
     "options": {
       "temperature": 0.0
     }
   }' | jq
   ```

   The model response

   ```json
   {
     "model": "llama3.1",
     "created_at": "2077-04-27T11:35:09.818149071Z",
     "message": {
       "role": "assistant",
       "content": "Humans first landed on the Moon on July 20, 1969. NASA's Apollo 11 mission successfully touched down on the lunar surface in the Sea of Tranquility (Latin: Mare Tranquillitatis) with astronauts Neil Armstrong and Edwin \"Buzz\" Aldrin becoming the first humans to set foot on the Moon.\n\nArmstrong famously declared, \"That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind,\" as he stepped off the lunar module Eagle onto the Moon's surface. The mission was a historic achievement that marked the culmination of years of hard work and dedication by thousands of people involved in the Apollo program.\n\nWould you like to know more about the Apollo 11 mission or the history of space exploration?"
     },
     "done": true,
     "done_reason": "stop",
     "total_duration": 12880145690,
     "load_duration": 1653962047,
     "prompt_eval_count": 19,
     "prompt_eval_duration": 478666931,
     "eval_count": 148,
     "eval_duration": 10651556622
   }
   ```

2. Build the application

   This step assumes that Ollama is accessible on port `11434` and that the
   `llama3.1` model is available. For further details, please refer to Step 1.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean verify
   ```

   (*Optional*) Verify that the application was created and the dependencies
   copied.

   ```shell
   tree --sort=name './target/libs'
   ```

   The application JAR file and its dependencies.

   ```
   ./target/libs
   ├── ai-services-langchain4j-ollama-api-1.0.0.jar
   ├── jackson-annotations-2.21.jar
   ├── jackson-core-2.21.1.jar
   ├── jackson-databind-2.21.1.jar
   ├── jspecify-1.0.0.jar
   ├── langchain4j-1.13.1.jar
   ├── langchain4j-core-1.13.1.jar
   ├── langchain4j-http-client-1.13.1.jar
   ├── langchain4j-http-client-jdk-1.13.1.jar
   ├── langchain4j-ollama-1.13.1.jar
   ├── logback-classic-1.5.32.jar
   ├── logback-core-1.5.32.jar
   ├── opennlp-tools-2.5.4.jar
   └── slf4j-api-2.0.17.jar

   1 directory, 14 files
   ```

3. Run the program

   This step assumes that Ollama is accessible on port `11434` and that the
   `llama3.1` model is available. For further details, please refer to Step 1.

   ```shell
   java \
     --class-path './target/libs/*' \
     demo.Main
   ```

   Although the prompt remains the same, the output may vary with each run.

   ```
   ---
   Summarisation Example
   text (1199)> The **Apollo 11 moon landing** was a historic spaceflight mission carried out by NASA, marking humanity’s first successful crewed landing on the Moon. Launched on **July 16, 1969**, from Kennedy Space Center, the spacecraft carried astronauts **Neil Armstrong**, **Buzz Aldrin**, and **Michael Collins**. After a three-day journey, the lunar module **Eagle** separated from the command module **Columbia** and descended toward the Moon’s surface. On **July 20, 1969**, at 20:17 UTC, Armstrong piloted the Eagle to a safe landing in the **Sea of Tranquility**.

   A few hours later, Armstrong became the first human to set foot on the lunar surface, declaring his famous words: **"That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind."** Aldrin soon joined him, and together they spent about **2.5 hours** exploring the surface, collecting rock samples, and setting up experiments. Meanwhile, Collins orbited the Moon in the command module, ensuring a safe return. The crew returned to Earth on **July 24, 1969**, splashing down in the Pacific Ocean. The Apollo 11 mission remains one of humanity’s greatest achievements, symbolizing technological innovation and the triumph of human exploration.

   summarised (437 36%)> Here is a summary of the text in two sentences:

   The Apollo 11 mission was a historic spaceflight that successfully landed astronauts Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin, and Michael Collins on the Moon's surface on July 20, 1969. The crew spent about 2.5 hours exploring the lunar surface, collecting samples, and conducting experiments before returning to Earth on July 24, marking one of humanity's greatest achievements in space exploration.
   ```
